professor.name: Dr. Harrington
professor.text: Economists disagree about whether a universal basic income—a regular payment to every citizen regardless of employment—would strengthen or weaken society. Would introducing such a policy be beneficial overall? Justify your position.

students.name: Nadia
students.text: It would be beneficial. As automation eliminates routine jobs, a basic income would give people the security to retrain or start businesses instead of accepting exploitative work.

students.name: Callum
students.text: I'm skeptical. Funding it would require enormous tax increases, and unconditional payments might reduce the incentive to contribute to society through work.

professor.name: Professor Feldman
professor.text: Some historians argue that studying the past helps us avoid repeating mistakes; others contend that every historical situation is unique, so lessons rarely transfer. To what extent can history guide present-day decisions?

students.name: Isabel
students.text: History is invaluable. Patterns such as how economic crises lead to political extremism recur often enough that recognizing them can help policymakers act earlier.

students.name: Tobias
students.text: The analogies are often misleading. Leaders frequently cite historical examples selectively to justify decisions they had already made.

professor.name: Dr. Lund
professor.text: Genetic testing companies now offer consumers detailed information about their ancestry and health risks. Do the benefits of this access outweigh the risks to privacy and wellbeing? Explain.

students.name: Priya
students.text: The benefits are significant. Knowing about a genetic risk early can lead to preventive care that saves lives.

students.name: Marcus
students.text: The risks are underestimated. Genetic data could be sold or hacked, and it affects relatives who never consented.

professor.name: Professor Achebe
professor.text: In many countries, a small number of elite universities produce a disproportionate share of political and business leaders. Is this concentration a problem for democratic societies? Why or why not?

students.name: Hannah
students.text: Yes. When leaders share the same background and networks, they are less likely to understand the experiences of ordinary citizens.

students.name: Rafael
students.text: Not necessarily. These institutions select talented people from many backgrounds, and excellence in leadership should be valued.

professor.name: Dr. Okonkwo
professor.text: Should wealthy nations prioritize reducing their own carbon emissions, or would it be more effective to finance emission reductions in developing countries? Defend your view.

students.name: Lea
students.text: Financing reductions abroad is often cheaper per ton of carbon, so the same money achieves more.

students.name: Jamal
students.text: Wealthy nations must cut their own emissions first; otherwise, paying others looks like buying the right to keep polluting.

professor.name: Professor Varga
professor.text: Some argue that standardized testing provides an objective measure of student achievement, while critics claim it narrows the curriculum and disadvantages certain groups. Should standardized tests play a major role in university admissions?

students.name: Oliver
students.text: Yes. Without common tests, admissions rely on grades that vary enormously between schools and on subjective essays.

students.name: Amira
students.text: No. Test scores correlate strongly with family income, so they reinforce inequality rather than measure potential.

professor.name: Dr. Silva
professor.text: Large technology companies collect vast amounts of personal data to provide free services. Should governments force these companies to pay users for their data? Explain your reasoning.

students.name: Felix
students.text: Yes. Our data generates enormous profits, and paying users would make the exchange fairer and more transparent.

students.name: Yuki
students.text: Payments would be tiny per person and might encourage people to sell even more sensitive information.

professor.name: Professor Holloway
professor.text: In an era of misinformation, should social media platforms be legally responsible for false content that users post? Discuss.

students.name: Grace
students.text: Yes. Platforms profit from engagement, including viral falsehoods, so they should bear responsibility for the harm.

students.name: Dmitri
students.text: Legal liability would push platforms to over-censor, silencing legitimate debate and minority opinions.

professor.name: Dr. Kowalski
professor.text: Research suggests that people are happier when they spend money on experiences rather than possessions. Should this finding influence public policy, for example through taxation? Why or why not?

students.name: Sofia
students.text: Possibly. Governments already use taxes to discourage harmful consumption, so encouraging wellbeing would be consistent.

students.name: Henrik
students.text: No. Happiness is personal, and it is not the state's role to decide how citizens should spend their money.

professor.name: Professor Mensah
professor.text: Many scientific studies cannot be replicated when other researchers repeat them. What does this 'replication crisis' suggest about how science should be funded and published?

students.name: Laura
students.text: Funders should reward replication studies, not only novel findings. Currently, there is no incentive to check others' work.

students.name: Kwame
students.text: Journals are the core problem. They prefer surprising results, which pushes researchers toward weak but exciting studies.

professor.name: Dr. Delacroix
professor.text: Should museums return artifacts that were taken from other countries during colonial periods? Consider both ethical and practical aspects.

students.name: Zainab
students.text: Yes. These objects are part of the cultural identity of the communities they were taken from.

students.name: Lucas
students.text: Each case is different. Some objects are better preserved and more widely seen in major museums.

professor.name: Professor Brandt
professor.text: Some cities have experimented with participatory budgeting, where residents vote directly on how part of the public budget is spent. Is this a good model for local democracy?

students.name: Elena
students.text: Yes. It increases civic engagement and ensures money goes to projects residents actually need.

students.name: Samir
students.text: Only active and well-organized groups tend to participate, so it can increase inequality between neighborhoods.

professor.name: Dr. Abara
professor.text: As life expectancy increases, should societies encourage people to work into their seventies? What are the social and economic implications?

students.name: Patrick
students.text: Longer working lives keep pension systems sustainable and allow experienced workers to mentor younger colleagues.

students.name: Mei
students.text: It could block opportunities for young people and is unfair to workers in physically demanding jobs.

professor.name: Professor Tanaka
professor.text: Is it ethical for companies to use behavioral psychology techniques—such as default options and nudges—to influence consumer decisions? Explain your position.

students.name: Chloe
students.text: It depends on the purpose. Nudging people to save for retirement is helpful; nudging them into subscriptions they forget to cancel is manipulative.

students.name: Anders
students.text: Any deliberate manipulation of decisions without people's awareness is ethically questionable, whatever the intention.

professor.name: Dr. Whitfield
professor.text: Many universities now offer degrees entirely online. Will online degrees eventually be valued as highly as traditional degrees by employers? Why or why not?

students.name: Noor
students.text: Yes. As top universities offer online programs, employers will focus on skills rather than the format of study.

students.name: Jakob
students.text: Traditional degrees will keep an advantage because they signal networking, discipline and campus experience.

professor.name: Professor Haddad
professor.text: Should governments impose strict limits on rent increases to address housing affordability, or would market-based solutions be more effective?

students.name: Ines
students.text: Rent controls protect tenants from sudden displacement and keep communities stable.

students.name: Martin
students.text: Economic evidence shows rent controls reduce housing supply. Building more homes is the real solution.

professor.name: Dr. Ivanova
professor.text: Some philosophers argue that we have moral obligations to future generations who do not yet exist. How should this idea affect current decisions about debt, resources and the environment?

students.name: Oskar
students.text: It should matter greatly. We are consuming resources and creating risks that future generations cannot vote on.

students.name: Adaeze
students.text: We cannot predict what future people will need, so we should focus on solving present injustices.

professor.name: Professor Abernathy
professor.text: Is the growing use of algorithms in criminal justice—for example, to predict reoffending—a step toward fairness or a threat to it?

students.name: Hugo
students.text: Algorithms can reduce human bias, since judges are influenced by fatigue and personal prejudice.

students.name: Leila
students.text: Algorithms trained on historical data reproduce past discrimination while appearing objective.

professor.name: Dr. Lindgren
professor.text: Should higher education focus primarily on preparing students for employment, or on developing critical thinking and broad knowledge? Defend your position.

students.name: Tara
students.text: Employability should be central. Students take on large debts and need degrees that lead to good jobs.

students.name: Viktor
students.text: Specific job skills become outdated quickly; critical thinking lasts a lifetime and adapts to change.

professor.name: Professor Okafor
professor.text: In many countries, a growing share of wealth is inherited rather than earned. Should inheritance taxes be significantly increased? Explain.

students.name: Clara
students.text: Yes. High inheritance taxes promote equal opportunity, because success should depend on effort rather than birth.

students.name: Ethan
students.text: People have a right to pass on what they have worked for, and high taxes may push wealth abroad.

professor.name: Dr. Feldman
professor.text: Some neuroscientists claim that adolescents' brains are not fully developed in areas related to judgment. Should this evidence affect the age at which young people are held fully responsible for crimes?

students.name: Ana
students.text: Yes. Legal systems should reflect scientific understanding and focus on rehabilitation for young offenders.

students.name: Benjamin
students.text: Brain development varies widely between individuals, so age-based rules based on averages are problematic.

professor.name: Professor Lund
professor.text: With the rise of machine translation, is it still worthwhile for students to invest years in learning foreign languages? Why or why not?

students.name: Riya
students.text: Absolutely. Language learning gives cultural insight and cognitive benefits that translation software cannot provide.

students.name: Thomas
students.text: For many practical purposes, translation tools are now sufficient, so the time could be spent on other skills.

professor.name: Dr. Henriksen
professor.text: Should public funding for the arts be based on popularity and audience numbers, or should it support work that may appeal only to small audiences? Explain.

students.name: Matteo
students.text: Public money should reflect public interest; funding popular work ensures taxpayers benefit.

students.name: Freya
students.text: The market already supports popular art. Public funding exists precisely to support experimental work that markets ignore.

professor.name: Professor Mensah
professor.text: Many companies claim to be 'carbon neutral' by buying carbon offsets. Are offsets a legitimate climate strategy or a form of greenwashing?

students.name: Sana
students.text: Well-regulated offsets, such as protecting forests, can play a useful role while companies transition.

students.name: Lukas
students.text: Many offset projects are unverifiable, and they let companies avoid the harder work of reducing emissions.

professor.name: Dr. Varga
professor.text: Is it more effective to address obesity through individual education campaigns or through regulation of the food industry? Defend your position.

students.name: Olivia
students.text: Regulation works better. Education has limited effect when unhealthy food is cheap and heavily advertised.

students.name: Arjun
students.text: Regulation alone is paternalistic; people need knowledge to make lasting changes in their habits.

professor.name: Professor Silva
professor.text: Some argue that remote work will lead to the decline of big cities as people move to smaller towns. Is this likely, and would it be desirable?

students.name: Kenji
students.text: It's happening already and could revitalize rural areas while reducing urban housing pressure.

students.name: Elise
students.text: Cities remain centers of culture and innovation; most people will still want the opportunities they offer.

professor.name: Dr. Holloway
professor.text: Should scientists engage in political advocacy on issues related to their research, such as climate change, or should they remain neutral providers of evidence?

students.name: Hassan
students.text: Scientists have a responsibility to speak out when their findings show serious risks to society.

students.name: Marta
students.text: Advocacy risks undermining public trust in science as an objective source of knowledge.

professor.name: Professor Kowalski
professor.text: Is economic growth compatible with environmental sustainability, or must wealthy countries accept lower growth to protect the planet?

students.name: Daniel
students.text: Green technology allows growth to be decoupled from emissions, as several countries have shown.

students.name: Aiko
students.text: Decoupling has been too slow. Endless growth on a finite planet is ultimately impossible.

professor.name: Dr. Achebe
professor.text: Should employers be allowed to require vaccination or other health measures as a condition of employment? Consider individual rights and collective safety.

students.name: Laila
students.text: In health care and schools, yes. Employers have a duty to protect vulnerable people.

students.name: Jonas
students.text: Medical decisions are personal; mandates can damage trust and should be a last resort.

professor.name: Professor Brandt
professor.text: Many young people today express interest in entrepreneurship rather than traditional careers. Should universities restructure programs to support start-up creation? Why or why not?

students.name: Lina
students.text: Yes. Incubators and entrepreneurship courses help translate research into innovations that benefit society.

students.name: Paul
students.text: Most start-ups fail; universities should not encourage students to take risks at the expense of their education.

professor.name: Dr. Abara
professor.text: Some researchers argue that constant smartphone use is reducing people's ability to concentrate. Should schools ban phones entirely during the school day?

students.name: Eva
students.text: A full ban is justified. Studies show even the presence of a phone reduces concentration.

students.name: Rami
students.text: Teaching responsible use is better preparation for adult life than prohibition.

professor.name: Professor Tanaka
professor.text: Is meritocracy—the idea that rewards should be based on talent and effort—a fair principle for organizing society, or does it hide structural inequalities?

students.name: Gabriel
students.text: Meritocracy is fairer than any alternative, such as rewarding connections or family status.

students.name: Nia
students.text: It ignores that talent and effort are shaped by circumstances, so it ends up justifying existing privilege.

professor.name: Dr. Whitfield
professor.text: Should governments subsidize nuclear energy as part of the transition away from fossil fuels? Explain your reasoning.

students.name: Stefan
students.text: Yes. Nuclear power provides reliable low-carbon electricity when wind and sun are unavailable.

students.name: Julia
students.text: Nuclear plants are expensive and slow to build; the money would achieve more in renewables and storage.

professor.name: Professor Haddad
professor.text: In your view, does globalization tend to strengthen or erode local cultures? Use examples.

students.name: Diego
students.text: It erodes them. Global brands and media gradually replace local traditions and languages.

students.name: Mina
students.text: It can strengthen them: global platforms allow local music and cuisine to reach new audiences.

professor.name: Dr. Ivanova
professor.text: Some argue that peer review is the foundation of trustworthy science; others say it is slow and conservative. How should scientific quality be ensured in the future?

students.name: Ruth
students.text: Peer review should remain but be made open, so reviewers' reasoning is transparent and accountable.

students.name: Kai
students.text: Preprints with public commentary allow faster and broader scrutiny than a few anonymous reviewers.

professor.name: Professor Abernathy
professor.text: Should companies be required to give employees a seat on their boards, as in some European countries? What would be the consequences?

students.name: Ingrid
students.text: Worker representation leads to more long-term decisions and better treatment of employees.

students.name: Owen
students.text: It may slow decision-making and conflict with shareholders' interests in competitive markets.

professor.name: Dr. Lindgren
professor.text: Is it justified for governments to restrict freedom of movement during public health emergencies? Where should the limits lie?

students.name: Hana
students.text: Temporary restrictions are justified when they clearly save lives, but they must be time-limited and reviewed.

students.name: Marco
students.text: Restrictions often outlast their purpose and disproportionately harm people with insecure jobs.

professor.name: Professor Okafor
professor.text: Many universities rely heavily on fees from international students. Is this financially and ethically sustainable?

students.name: Wei
students.text: It benefits everyone: international students gain education, and universities can fund research.

students.name: Charlotte
students.text: Relying on high fees treats international students as revenue sources and makes universities vulnerable to sudden drops in enrollment.

professor.name: Dr. Feldman
professor.text: Should the use of performance-enhancing technologies, such as advanced prosthetics or gene therapies, be allowed in professional sport?

students.name: Diana
students.text: Sport should celebrate natural human ability; technological enhancements make competition meaningless.

students.name: Jonah
students.text: Sport has always used technology—better shoes, training methods. Banning new enhancements is arbitrary.

professor.name: Professor Lund
professor.text: Is it the role of schools to teach moral values, or should this be left to families and communities?

students.name: Amina
students.text: Schools must teach shared values like respect and honesty, because not all children learn them at home.

students.name: Erik
students.text: In diverse societies, schools should teach critical reasoning and let families transmit their own values.

professor.name: Dr. Mensah
professor.text: Some economists propose a tax on financial transactions to reduce speculation. Would this make financial markets more stable or simply reduce efficiency?

students.name: Simon
students.text: A small tax would discourage harmful short-term trading without affecting long-term investors.

students.name: Leonie
students.text: It would raise costs for ordinary savers and push trading to countries without the tax.

professor.name: Professor Delacroix
professor.text: In many countries, fewer people are reading literature for pleasure. Does this matter for society? Why or why not?

students.name: Sophie
students.text: It matters. Reading fiction develops empathy and the ability to follow complex arguments.

students.name: Rahul
students.text: People still engage with stories through films, games and podcasts; the format is changing, not the value.

professor.name: Dr. Varga
professor.text: Should cities prioritize building affordable housing in central areas, even if this means fewer green spaces? Explain your view.

students.name: Anja
students.text: Housing near jobs reduces commuting and inequality, which outweighs the loss of some parks.

students.name: Yusuf
students.text: Green spaces are essential for public health; housing should be built on underused land instead.

professor.name: Professor Silva
professor.text: Is it ethical for wealthy individuals to fund major public projects, such as hospitals or space programs, rather than paying higher taxes?

students.name: Lars
students.text: Philanthropy can be faster and more innovative than government spending.

students.name: Fatima
students.text: It gives private individuals too much influence over public priorities without democratic accountability.

professor.name: Dr. Holloway
professor.text: Should artificial intelligence systems be allowed to make medical diagnoses without a human doctor's approval?

students.name: Victor
students.text: In some areas, AI already outperforms doctors; requiring approval may slow down life-saving care.

students.name: Leah
students.text: Medicine involves responsibility and communication; a human must remain accountable for decisions.

professor.name: Professor Kowalski
professor.text: Some countries offer financial incentives to encourage people to have more children. Are such policies an appropriate response to declining birth rates?

students.name: Elena
students.text: Incentives like childcare support help families who want children but cannot afford them.

students.name: Ahmed
students.text: Cash incentives have shown limited effects; immigration and productivity are more realistic responses.

professor.name: Dr. Achebe
professor.text: Should universities publicly rank their professors based on student evaluations and research output? Why or why not?

students.name: Nora
students.text: Transparency would encourage better teaching and help students choose courses.

students.name: Patrick
students.text: Rankings oversimplify complex work and could discourage professors from teaching difficult but valuable courses.

professor.name: Professor Brandt
professor.text: Is consumer boycotting an effective way to change corporate behavior? Use examples to support your view.

students.name: Ivy
students.text: Yes. Several companies changed their labor practices after boycotts damaged their reputations.

students.name: Tomas
students.text: Most boycotts fade quickly; legislation is more reliable than consumer pressure.

professor.name: Dr. Abara
professor.text: Should people have a 'right to disconnect'—a legal right to ignore work communications outside working hours?

students.name: Luisa
students.text: Yes. Constant availability causes burnout, and the law should protect employees' private time.

students.name: Ben
students.text: Some jobs require flexibility, and many workers prefer to answer messages when it suits them.

professor.name: Professor Tanaka
professor.text: Some argue that preserving biodiversity is a moral duty, while others justify it mainly by its economic value. Which justification is more convincing, and does it matter?

students.name: Moana
students.text: The moral argument is stronger: species have value in themselves, not just as resources for humans.

students.name: Daniel
students.text: Economic arguments are more persuasive for policymakers, so they are more useful in practice.
